newsitem.title: UK: Mideast VLCCs look up after bearish week.
newsitem.headline: Mideast VLCCs look up after bearish week.

text.p: Middle East very large crude carrier (VLCC) rates showed signs of picking up on Monday after a bearish week that was dominated by a buildup of tonnage and a surfeit of Far Eastern re-lets which overshadowed good enquiry, brokers said.
They said rates were now holding at W47.5 to most destinations after dipping as low as W45 last week, and there now seemed to be scope for a recovery.
"We should now see the market improve. There is now more of a balance between enquiries and vessels with the surplus tonnage we saw last week starting to dry up," one VLCC broker said.
Another broker said a bottom seemed to have been reached, and that last week's low of about W45 was some five points above the bottom for this time last year.
He noted that in 1996 rates shot up after hitting bottom, approaching W80 for Mideast/Japan in June, and he did not rule out this happening again this year.
In contrast, the Caribs/upcoast crude tanker market dived to W185 from about W210 on Friday and after a spectacular bull run in recent weeks.
A U.S. broker said the fall was due to plenty of ships in fairly prompt positions.
"I think it's going to soften relatively rapidly but not crater," he added. "We could be down to the 170s by the end of the week."
Upcoast 70,000 tonne cargoes have zigzagged in recent months, hitting a year high of W244.69 and a low of just W115.02, according to Reuters data.
The West Africa/U.S. Gulf market was quiet, with VLCCs still at a mediocre W62.5, pushed down by the sluggish Middle sector, and with 130,000 tonne vessels (Suezmaxes) unchanged at W92.5.
Transatlantic VLCCs were also little changed and inactive at W65 with Suezmaxes at W87.5/90.
In the Mediterranean, 80,000 tonne vessels (Aframaxes) were holding at about W105, but an Italian broker said, "I believe this level could be set to fall a bit as there isn't much activity."
He was no more optimistic about Suezmaxes, even though this sector was more active and currently steady at W92.5, as there was ample tonnage available.
The inter-U.K./Cont market was also depressed by plentiful tonnage and re-lets, especially from Shell, another broker said.
"Charterers are trying to push rates lower. The pressure is on -- there are too many ships and not enough cargoes," he added. He put 80,000 tonne UKC cargoes unchanged for now at W92.5.
Fuel oil rates were unchanged, with 25,000 tonne inter-UKC cargoes at W185 and cross-Med at W195.
